title: Coaching by Numbers
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles argues that school leaders and teachers alike hold strong opinions on everything and rarely test them, which is a problem for coaching and decision-making. He cites evidence that observers misjudge lesson quality and a decline in progress scores at research schools to show how unreliable confident opinion is. His answer, Coaching by Numbers, is to put a count on an opinion before coaching, for example counting students who complete retrieval tasks or tallying who answers each question. He works through six scenarios covering task completion, visualiser use, cold calling, exam mark allocation, retrieval planning and club versus tutoring time. In each, the numbers shift the conversation toward what the teacher or leader actually wants. He ends with his own case of split classes, where counted opinions were wrong and standardised results showed greater progress.
points: Salles claims leaders and teachers are overconfident in their opinions, citing lesson-observation research in which 63 percent of judgements are wrong.
His method pairs a number with each opinion, then uses coaching questions to let the teacher decide what number counts as acceptable.
He suggests a habit-forming prompt such as popping in for 10 to 30 seconds over three weeks to ask whether the class is working and thinking hard.
He shows how counting marks, lessons and retrieval opportunities can expose curriculum pacing and time-use trade-offs, such as clubs versus small-group tutoring.
His split-class example shows his team's unanimous opinion was wrong once progress data was examined.
quotes: This is a real problem for leaders. How do you know your idea is as good as you think it is? It is a problem for teachers: how do you know your leader’s idea is as poor as you think it is? Rather than knowing, both are likely to simply have very strong opinions.

Becoming a research school appears to reduce student progress. There may be multiple reasons for this, but the most obvious one is that even great ideas are hard to scale. We end up applying research in ways which fit our opinions rather than the facts.

You notice that the teacher defaults to questioning volunteers. This lack of cold call, you think, means that students don’t have to think hard and misconceptions are not identified (as volunteers usually know the right answer).

Instead, go through each individual question, with the mark scheme, and itemise what marks are actually given for knowledge in each question. For example, a 12 mark ‘application’ question may well award the first 5 marks simply for factual knowledge.

Once you know how many lessons and homeworks there are, you have the total number of retrieval opportunities. Let’s say there are 25 quotations for each text, and 4 texts, giving 100 quotations, and these need to be retrieved 6 times each, then there are 600 questions. So for literature, there might be 60-65 weeks of KS4 lessons, (depending on student absence) which means that students will need to retrieve 10 quotations every week. Now do the same for all the other essential knowledge, and you have a clear sequence of what should be retrieved when.
For every opinion you hold dear, and every change proposed to your working day, try to put a number on it. Link that number to progress.

But, this simply counted opinions. It didn’t actually count progress. Once we looked at the results of our standardised assessments we found that the classes split between 3 teachers made most progress, then the classes shared between 2 teachers and finally, classes taught by just one teacher made the least progress (even though all classes were positive).
